\title{\textbf{A Living Dataset of International Influence}\\
\author{Raymond Hicks\thanks{Corresponding author: \href{mailto:arpie71@gmail.com}{arpie71@gmail.com}. Working paper; comments welcome. Code and data: the \texttt{gifts} repository. [Co-author names and affiliations to be added.]}}
\date{Working paper --- October 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent How can researchers measure the changing networks through which international influence operates? This paper introduces a living dataset of reported contacts between foreign officials and U.S. government personnel from 1999 to 2023. The underlying records come from annual Foreign Gifts and Decorations Act reports, but the paper treats individual gifts as observable traces of broader relationships: meetings, protocol exchanges, institutional connections, and repeated contact between bureaucracies. The central contribution is an infrastructure for studying these relationships over time. Each foreign and U.S. official is linked to a persistent Wikidata identifier, allowing the dataset to distinguish individuals from offices, follow officials across careers, connect them to external sources, and refresh information as those sources change. The resulting data contain 10,428 reported contacts involving 1,026 U.S. recipients, 2,361 foreign officials, 169 countries, and 107 U.S. agency units. We use the data to construct longitudinal person-level and institutional networks and to examine how bureaucratic roles, professional backgrounds, education, military service, and career mobility structure international contact. Drawing on the revolving-door literature, we argue that influence travels not only through formal institutions but also through the movement and connection of personnel across offices, agencies, and national systems. The dataset provides a platform for studying how those networks form, persist, and change.
\end{abstract}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} foreign gifts, bureaucrats, homophily, diplomacy, living data, Wikidata, record linkage, political elites

\hrule

\section{Introduction}


A Living Dataset of International Influence



Who carries influence across bureaucratic networks: the person, the career, or the office? Research on international politics increasingly shows that individual bureaucrats matter. International staff, diplomats, experts, and policy entrepreneurs shape agenda-setting, implementation, knowledge production, and institutional change \citep{barnett2004rules,heinzel2022,lang2025,clark2026bureaucratic}. Yet the growing emphasis on individual agency leaves open a basic question: does influence follow individuals as they move across institutions, or does it attach primarily to the formal positions they occupy?

Recent work conceptualizes individuals as structurally embedded actors. Their decisions reflect overlapping pressures associated with formal authority, organizational culture, professional networks, national affiliations, and career incentives \citep{weaver2026bringing}. This framework challenges accounts that treat bureaucratic influence as either a simple consequence of organizational position or an attribute of individual expertise. It also directs attention to a central empirical problem: people who occupy similar offices may face different pressures, while the same person may behave differently after moving across institutions.

This article examines that problem through a longitudinal dataset of bureaucratic interactions. We use diplomatic gifts not as an object of substantive interest in themselves, but as systematic records of encounters among individuals, agencies, governments, and organizations. By linking these records to individual identifiers, organizational affiliations, offices, and career histories, we ask whether interaction networks travel with people or remain attached to the organizations and positions they occupy.

The analysis advances three claims. First, position dominates career. Interaction counts are strongly associated with formal office, especially cabinet-level status, but not with career length, prior mobility, or accumulated professional history. This pattern holds both across individuals and within individuals as they move between positions. The finding qualifies the view that accumulated experience or extensive career networks necessarily generate greater influence. In this setting, bureaucratic influence appears to derive primarily from the authority, visibility, and access attached to the current office.

Second, organizations retain foreign relationships when the personnel who carried them leave. When all observed personnel associated with an agency-country relationship depart, the relationship itself becomes less likely to recur. Yet its recurrence through other personnel does not decline appreciably. The departing individual’s own contact is lost, but the organization’s broader relationship persists through successors. This suggests that institutional continuity depends less on the permanent presence of particular individuals than on organizational routines, records, expectations, and positional access.

Third, brokerage is concentrated and positional. Individuals who connect otherwise separate agencies, countries, or professional communities are overwhelmingly senior officials. Apparent links between career mobility and brokerage largely disappear when compared with degree-preserving null networks, indicating that mobility may appear to generate brokerage because mobile or prominent individuals simply have more ties. Below the cabinet level, brokerage is concentrated among military service chiefs, protocol officers, defense officials, and senior legislators serving on foreign-affairs and armed-services committees. These are not random career generalists; they occupy offices that structurally connect domestic authority to international interaction.

Together, these findings qualify both leader-centered and career-centered accounts of bureaucratic influence. The relevant contrast is not between individuals and institutions, but between person-carried and position-carried influence. Individuals can matter, particularly when they connect organizations or retain relationships after moving. However, the empirical pattern suggests that most observed interaction is generated by formal office and organizational location. The organization does not simply aggregate the preferences and networks of its personnel; it provides the institutional platform that makes particular forms of access possible.

This paper develops a new data infrastructure for studying those questions. We transform annual reports published under the Foreign Gifts and Decorations Act into a longitudinal record of international contact involving U.S. officials and foreign representatives. The reports identify individuals, offices, agencies, countries, dates, and circumstances associated with reported exchanges. We do not treat any particular exchange as a direct measure of influence. Instead, we use each observation as an observable trace of contact that can be linked to information about the people and institutions involved. Aggregated over time, these traces reveal networks of interaction across agencies, bureaucracies, countries, and professional communities.

The project’s theoretical motivation comes from research on bureaucratic careers, elite networks, and revolving doors. Existing work often examines movement between public and private employment or the consequences of post-government careers \citep{carnes2023economic,lewis2008politics,teodoro2011bureaucratic}. Our data extend this perspective to connections among public officials across national and organizational boundaries. They capture interactions among diplomats, military officers, intelligence personnel, legislators, civil servants, and other technical officials. Because the records span twenty-five years, they also allow us to study networks as processes rather than fixed structures. We can ask whether contact follows the office, the person, the career, the institution, or an earlier relationship—and how those patterns change as agencies, administrations, and international conditions change.

To this end, we build a living dataset rather than a static historical file. This approach rebuilding from primary sources whenever new material appears; stores human judgments in versioned lookup files; links people and organizations to persistent identifiers; and preserves the code, source files, and decisions needed to reproduce each release. This setup holds particular benefits for individual-level research. The same official may appear under different names, titles, spellings, transliterations, and offices. A person may serve as a legislator, ambassador, cabinet official, agency head, or military commander over the course of a career. Without a persistent identifier, researchers cannot reliably distinguish office from officeholder or determine whether apparently separate observations concern the same individual.

We use Wikidata identifiers to address this problem \citep{vrandecic2014wikidata}. Each linked person receives a Wikidata identifier, or QID, which allows the dataset to connect contact records to information on positions held, dates of service, education, occupation, military experience, employers, party membership, and family relationships. The identifier also makes the dataset extensible: researchers can join it to other person-level datasets, including the Comparative Legislators Database \citep[CLD;][]{gobel2022cld}, update contextual information as Wikidata changes, and follow individuals as they move across organizations. The paper therefore contributes not simply a new collection of observations, but a reusable framework for building longitudinal networks of political and bureaucratic contact.

The data support a substantive shift in emphasis. Rather than asking primarily who gave the most valuable gifts, we ask which agencies and bureaucracies interact with which foreign counterparts, which connections persist over time, and whether contact reflects institutional matching or person-level affinity. Do military agencies interact disproportionately with foreign military establishments because of formal counterpart relationships? Do diplomats maintain cross-national networks after moving between postings? Do officials with shared education, professional training, or career experience appear in the same contact networks? Do changes in administration, conflict, or organizational structure alter these patterns? These questions concern influence, access, and institutional connectivity—not the intrinsic meaning of any particular object exchanged.

The empirical analysis proceeds at three levels. First, we describe the temporal structure of reported contact across U.S. agencies, branches, countries, and foreign institutions. Second, we use persistent identifiers to construct person-level networks and follow officials across offices and careers. Third, we compare the professional, educational, and institutional characteristics of connected officials, using random-pairing baselines to distinguish ordinary institutional matching from person-level similarity. We draw on research showing that social ties form disproportionately among similar people \citep{mcpherson2001birds}, that personal rapport can shape diplomacy \citep{holmes2013force}, and that universities and military colleges connect national elites across borders \citep{atkinson2010soft,ruby2010pme,gift2017who}.

The analysis is descriptive and exploratory. The data identify patterns of contact and possible relational infrastructure, but they do not by themselves establish that any exchange caused a policy decision or generated influence. Nor can the reports capture every meeting, relationship, or channel of communication. Reporting practices differ across agencies, some records withhold the identity of foreign officials, and the existence of an observed exchange does not reveal what either party intended. These limitations make the dataset an imperfect but valuable starting point for studying the observable institutional traces of international networks.

Our current release contains 10,428 reported contacts involving 1,026 linked U.S. recipients, 2,361 linked foreign officials, 169 countries, and 107 agency units. We show that most observed similarity between foreign officials and U.S. recipients reflects institutional matching: military personnel interact with military organizations, diplomats with diplomatic agencies, and officials in particular branches encounter characteristic foreign counterparts. At the same time, person-level similarities in professional background, birth cohort, and education appear above branch- and year-specific baselines. These patterns suggest that formal offices organize international contact, while individual careers and networks shape how those connections persist and change.

The broader aim is to make international influence more observable. By combining living-data principles, Wikidata-based entity resolution, longitudinal network analysis, and theories of bureaucratic mobility and revolving doors, the project offers a way to study how people—not only states or institutions—carry relationships across organizational and national boundaries.

\section{Theory: Careers, Structural Embedding, and Bureaucratic Influence}

Theory: Position, Career, and Organizational Continuity

The contemporary literature on bureaucratic influence emphasizes that international outcomes are shaped by actors embedded within formal organizations and overlapping professional structures. Clark, Dolan, and Jost identify bureaucratic selection and decision-making centralization as key conditions governing influence \citep{clark2026bureaucratic}. Weaver, Morrison, and Heinzel similarly argue that individuals face different combinations of structural pressures depending on their affiliations, identities, institutional settings, and professional histories \citep{weaver2026bringing}. Heinzel, Weaver, and Jorgensen show how the composition and representation of international bureaucracies can affect organizational priorities, illustrating that staff characteristics matter through their interaction with institutional roles and organizational processes \citep{heinzel2025bureaucratic}.

These arguments generate two competing expectations. A career-centered account predicts that influence accumulates through experience, mobility, and repeated interaction. Individuals who have worked in many organizations should possess more extensive networks, greater institutional knowledge, and more opportunities to broker across organizational boundaries. Their prior relationships should follow them as they move, allowing them to carry connections from one agency to another.

A position-centered account predicts that influence attaches primarily to formal office. Cabinet officials, agency heads, military chiefs, protocol officers, and senior legislators receive more interaction because their offices confer authority, visibility, access, and symbolic importance. From this perspective, personnel movement should matter less than the institutional position a person occupies at a given moment. The same individual should receive more interaction when holding a prominent office and less when holding a less visible position, even if the person’s accumulated career history remains constant.

The distinction is consequential because the two accounts imply different mechanisms of institutional influence. If career dominates, organizations are partly containers for person-specific networks. When an official moves, relationships, expertise, and influence should move with them. If position dominates, organizations are more than containers: they structure access independently of the individual who occupies the role. Personnel may change while the organization’s external relationships persist because successors inherit the office, the organizational mandate, and the routines through which contact occurs.

The first hypothesis is therefore:

H1: Interaction volume is more strongly associated with formal position than with career length, prior mobility, or accumulated professional history.

This hypothesis has both between-person and within-person implications. Between people, cabinet-level officials should receive more interactions than legislators, agency staff, military personnel, or diplomats, even after accounting for career length and prior appearances. Within people, an individual’s interaction rate should change when the person enters or leaves a prominent office. Evidence of both patterns would suggest that formal position, rather than stable individual characteristics, drives the observed interaction volume.

The second hypothesis concerns institutional continuity:

H2: When personnel associated with an agency-country relationship leave, the relationship will continue through other personnel at approximately the same rate.

This hypothesis does not imply that individuals are irrelevant. A departing person’s own contacts may disappear, and some relationships may be partially person-carried. But if organizations retain foreign relationships through routines, records, successor access, and institutional expectations, then other personnel should continue the relationship after the original carrier departs. The relevant comparison is therefore not whether the relationship recurs at all, but whether it recurs through the same individual or through the organization’s other personnel.

This distinction follows from the broader literature’s emphasis on organizational processes. International bureaucracies develop cultures, routines, and forms of expertise that can outlast individual staff members \citep{barnett2004rules,weaver2016,murdoch2019}. Heinzel and colleagues likewise show that bureaucratic characteristics matter through organizational processes rather than through individual attributes alone \citep{heinzel2022,heinzel2025bureaucratic}. If institutional relationships are embedded in organizational practice, turnover should not necessarily dissolve them.

The third hypothesis concerns brokerage:

H3: Brokerage is concentrated among individuals occupying positions that structurally connect organizations, countries, or domestic and international authority.

A career-centered account predicts that mobility itself produces brokerage. Officials who have moved across agencies and sectors should connect otherwise separate communities. A positional account predicts that apparent mobility effects will largely disappear once the number of ties is held constant and observed networks are compared with appropriate null graphs. Brokerage should instead be concentrated among offices that routinely connect institutional domains: cabinet positions, military commands, protocol offices, foreign-affairs committees, and senior diplomatic posts.

This expectation also follows from the embedded-agent framework. Individuals do not encounter structural pressures independently of their offices. Their professional histories may shape how they interpret those pressures, but formal roles determine which interactions are available in the first place \citep{weaver2026bringing}. A military service chief or protocol officer may become a broker not because of unusually extensive prior mobility, but because the office itself sits at the intersection of domestic authority, diplomacy, and foreign representation.

The theory therefore distinguishes three mechanisms:

Person-carried influence: relationships, expertise, or access that follow an individual across institutional transitions.

Position-carried influence: interactions generated by the authority, visibility, and institutional access attached to a formal office.

Organization-carried influence: relationships that persist because agencies retain routines, records, mandates, and successor personnel capable of maintaining them.

These mechanisms are not mutually exclusive. The empirical question is their relative importance. A modest person-carried component may coexist with strong organizational continuity. Likewise, a mobile individual may become a broker, but only because the new position provides the authority and access necessary to activate prior relationships.

This framework also clarifies what static datasets cannot observe. A cross-sectional dataset can show that cabinet officials receive more interactions than agency staff, but it cannot establish whether this difference reflects individual reputation, career history, or the formal office. A dataset organized only around organizations can show that an agency maintains foreign relationships, but it cannot reveal whether those relationships persist through the same people or through successors. A static network can identify central actors, but it cannot determine whether brokerage reflects genuine mobility, accumulated ties, or simply degree and prominence.

The longitudinal data allow these mechanisms to be separated. Person-level comparisons identify differences across career types. Within-person transitions show whether interaction changes when the same individual enters a different office. Organization-level turnover tests whether foreign ties persist after personnel change. Tie-level analyses distinguish recurrence through the original carrier from recurrence through other personnel. Finally, degree-preserving permutation tests assess whether the association between career mobility and brokerage exceeds what would be expected from the number of connections alone.

The resulting argument is deliberately narrower than a general claim that bureaucrats do not matter. Individuals matter, but their influence is structured by formal position and organizational context. Career history and mobility may create a modest person-carried component, particularly for selected relationships and brokerage positions. Yet the dominant empirical pattern is that interaction follows the office, while organizations preserve their external ties through personnel change. This suggests that bureaucratic influence is neither wholly individual nor wholly institutional: it is positional in its concentration, organizational in its continuity, and only selectively personal in its transmission.


\section{What Is a Living Dataset?}\label{sec:living}

\begin{sidebar}{Living dataset}
A \textbf{living dataset} is a continuously updating collection of data that evolves over time rather than remaining frozen in a static state. Concretely, (\emph{a}) it is rebuilt from primary sources by code whenever those sources change; (\emph{b}) human judgments (for example, ``this \emph{Abdullah} is \qid{Q57464}'') are stored as data in versioned lookup tables, so they persist across rebuilds instead of being redone; (\emph{c}) entities are keyed by persistent identifiers maintained outside the project, so linked attributes can be refreshed; and (\emph{d}) each release is reproducible, so a result can be traced to a specific version of sources, lookups, and code.
\end{sidebar}

Most datasets in political science are \emph{static}: a team codes a population over a fixed window, deposits a file, and moves on. Static datasets are valuable and often superb, but they carry two familiar costs.

\paragraph{Static data are hard to merge.} A dataset built around names, or around project-specific numeric codes, can be joined to another only through a crosswalk that someone must build. For countries this problem is largely solved by shared code systems and the tools that translate among them \citep{arelbundock2018countrycode}. For individuals it is not. Names are transliterated in many ways (the lookup file maps eleven distinct name strings, among them \emph{Abdelazia}, \emph{Abdelkaziz}, and \emph{Bonteflika}, to Abdelaziz Bouteflika's single QID), titles are folded into names, and the same person appears under different offices. Researchers therefore fall back on fuzzy or probabilistic record linkage \citep{enamorado2019using}. That is feasible but costly, and every research team repeats it with slightly different results.

\paragraph{Static data are hard to update.} When a source adds a year, a static dataset either goes out of date or must be reconstructed, often by different people with different rules. The cleaning decisions embedded in the original release (which rows were dropped, how ambiguous names were resolved) are frequently lost. The transparency and replication literature has long noted this problem \citep{king1995replication,lupia2014openness}. Event datasets such as GDELT \citep{leetaru2013gdelt} show the opposite pole: fully automated and continuously updated, but with limited human verification of who the actors are.

A living dataset sits between these poles. Updating is routine because the pipeline, not a person, does the repetitive work. Human verification is cumulative because it is stored in lookup files the pipeline consults on every run. Merging is cheap because entities are keyed to an external, community-maintained identifier. These features map closely onto the FAIR principles of findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability \citep{wilkinson2016fair}. The persistent identifier is what makes the data interoperable.

The gift reports suit this model particularly well. They arrive on a predictable annual cycle, roughly a year after the calendar year they cover: the report for calendar year 2024 appeared on January 29, 2026 \citep{fr2026gifts}. Their format drifts from year to year, but not by much. And most of their actors are exactly the kind of internationally prominent people Wikidata describes well.

\section{The Source: Foreign Gift Reports}\label{sec:source}

The U.S.\ Constitution's foreign emoluments clause bars federal officers from accepting any ``present'' from a foreign state without the consent of Congress. The Foreign Gifts and Decorations Act of 1966, codified at 5 U.S.C.\ \S\,7342, supplies that consent in a structured form. Employees may accept gifts of ``minimal value'' (a threshold the General Services Administration revises every three years to track the consumer price index: \$390 for 2017--2019, \$415 for 2020--2022, and \$480 for 2023--2025; \citealt{gsa2023minimal}). Gifts above the threshold may be accepted when refusing would ``cause offense or embarrassment or otherwise adversely affect the foreign relations of the United States,'' but they become property of the United States and must be reported. Each employing agency compiles these reports, and the State Department publishes the combined list annually. The statute's definition of ``foreign government'' includes international organizations, so the World Health Organization and NATO bodies appear as givers alongside heads of state. Agencies may also withhold the giver's identity when publishing it would harm intelligence sources (\S\,7342(f)(4)). We return to this below.

The project does not treat gifts as intrinsically important objects or seek to explain gift-giving as an isolated diplomatic practice. Instead, gifts provide unusually systematic records of interactions among individuals, agencies, governments, and international organizations, often identifying participants, institutional affiliations, dates, locations, and the context of an encounter. The substantive object of interest is therefore not the gift itself but the interaction it records: repeated exchanges can reveal who meets whom, which agencies interact, how relationships persist across changes in office, and whether particular individuals connect otherwise separate institutional communities. By linking these records to individual identifiers, career histories, organizational affiliations, and subsequent meetings, the project uses gift data to study the formation, maintenance, and transformation of bureaucratic networks over time.

Each published entry has four fields:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Recipient}: name, title, and often the organization (``Admiral John Richardson, U.S.\ Navy, Chief of Naval Operations'');
\item \textbf{Gift}: a free-text block that packs together the description of the item, the date received, the estimated value, and the disposition (``\ldots{} Rec'd---August 28, 2002. Est.\ Value---\$1,000,000. Archives Foreign'');
\item \textbf{Giver}: honorific, name, title, and country (``His Royal Highness Prince Bandar bin Sultan, Ambassador of Saudi Arabia'');
\item \textbf{Circumstances}: the justification for acceptance (most often the non-embarrassment clause).
\end{itemize}
Entries are grouped into agency sections, such as ``The White House---Executive Office of the President,'' ``Department of the Navy,'' and ``United States Senate,'' and the grouping is itself informative. The reports are published as structured XML, which we use, though the content of each cell is free text.



Most of the people in these records are not elected. Ambassadors, assistant secretaries, admirals, generals, and agency heads together receive more gifts than presidents and members of Congress, and each gift names both the American official and the foreign official who presented it. The records therefore let us ask two questions about the bureaucracy that are hard to answer elsewhere. First, \emph{who} are the American officials that foreign governments cultivate, and how do they differ across the diplomatic, defense, intelligence, and domestic agencies? Second, \emph{what do givers and recipients share}? Social ties form disproportionately among similar people \citep{mcpherson2001birds}, personal rapport is a resource in diplomacy \citep{holmes2013force}, and American universities and military colleges have trained a large share of the world's elites \citep{atkinson2010soft,ruby2010pme,gift2017who}. If foreign governments direct gifts toward officials who resemble their own representatives, by career, generation, or schooling, then the gift record captures relationships that run between people and not only between offices. Answering either question requires knowing much more about givers and recipients than the gift reports contain.

Table~\ref{tab:pipeline} summarizes the pipeline. Each stage reads the output of the previous one, so a new annual report can be added with one download command and one rebuild.

Stage & Script & What it does \\
\midrule
1.\ Acquire & \texttt{download\_data.py} & Fetches the Federal Register XML for a report year (URLs kept in \texttt{files/urls.csv}); archives the XML; writes one raw CSV per year. \\
2.\ Parse & \texttt{parseandclean\_new.py} & Forward-fills recipient and giver across multi-item listings; splits the gift blob into item, receipt date, value, disposition, location; splits names from honorifics, ranks, titles, and organizations; standardizes dates. \\

The countries of the educational institutions are looked up once and cached. \\
5.\ Analyze & \texttt{analysis/build\_analysis\_data.py} & Recovers the reporting agency from the XML section headings and groups agencies into branches; assigns giver country and giver type; builds person-level edge lists and a balanced country-year panel. \\

\subsection{Acquisition and Parsing}

The reports are published in the \emph{Federal Register} without a dedicated landing page, so each year's XML URL is recorded once in \texttt{files/urls.csv}. The download step stores both the original XML and a raw CSV, so later stages can return to the source. Parsing is mostly regular-expression work, but three features of the source deserve mention because they recur in other government registers.

\emph{First}, multi-item listings name the recipient and giver once and leave later rows blank; forward-filling restores the pair for each item. \emph{Second}, the gift field packs several variables into one string, and the labels drift across years (``Est.\ Value---,'' ``Estimated Value:,'' ``Appraised Value''). The parser peels labeled fields off the end of the string. Where a disposition appears without a label (``\$280.\ Government Property''), the parser does not try to enumerate the open-ended set of disposition phrases. It instead reads the value expression, whose vocabulary is closed (currency amounts, ``each,'' ``approximately,'' punctuation), and treats whatever follows as the disposition. \emph{Third}, honorifics and ranks (``His Excellency,'' ``The Right Honorable,'' ``Admiral'') are split from names before matching, because they otherwise defeat any name lookup.

\subsection{Entity Resolution to Wikidata}

Name resolution is deliberately \emph{semi}-automated. For each name without a QID, a SPARQL query returns Wikidata humans whose label or alias matches. A human then confirms, rejects, or corrects the candidates. Fully automated matching is unsafe: a query for ``Qin Gang'' returns five people. Confirmed matches are written to a master lookup file (\texttt{masterwiki\_new.csv}, currently about 4,700 name-to-QID mappings). Names that are confirmed to have no Wikidata item are written to an exclusion list, so they are not searched again. Non-person givers and recipients receive explicit codes: \texttt{FAMILY} for joint gifts from a royal couple, \texttt{GROUP} for delegations, \texttt{UNCLEAR} for unresolvable cases, and \texttt{NIL} for statutory placeholders such as ``5 U.S.C.\ 7342(f)(4).'' This separates ``not yet looked up'' from ``looked up and not a person,'' a distinction a living dataset needs.

Recipients recorded only by role (``President,'' ``Vice President,'' ``First Lady'') are resolved by year to the person who held the role. This is the first, simplest instance of the office/officeholder distinction we develop in Section~\ref{sec:office}.

\subsection{Recovering the Reporting Agency}

The reporting agency is not a field in the parsed data, but the XML encodes it. From 2001 onward each agency's table carries a title (\texttt{<TTITLE>Agency: Department of the Navy</TTITLE>}). In 1999 and 2000 the agency appears as a one-cell row inside a single long table. Walking the XML rows in document order assigns every gift to an agency. All \ngifts{} records receive one, under 107 distinct labels, which we group into seven branches: White House (including the Office of the Vice President and the National Security Council), Diplomatic (State, USAID), Defense (the department, the services, and combatant commands), Intelligence (CIA, ODNI, DIA), Legislative (House, Senate, GAO), Judicial, and Other executive. The agency tells us \emph{which institution} reported the gift; the recipient's QID tells us \emph{who} received it.

\subsection{Giver Country and Giver Type}

We assign each gift a giving country from the text of the giver field, which almost always names the government (``\ldots{} King of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia''). Where the text names no country, we fall back on the giver's Wikidata country of citizenship (P27). Regime-specific Wikidata items (``Islamic Republic of Afghanistan,'' ``Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya'') are folded into the continuing state, so each country keeps a single identifier and ISO~3166 code across the panel. This yields a country for 84\% of gifts. Nearly all of the rest are gifts with a withheld giver identity or gifts from international organizations, which we code as their own giver type. As a check, where both sources are available (more than 5,000 gifts), the text-based country and the Wikidata citizenship agree 99\% of the time. We also classify the giver's role from honorifics and titles: royalty, head of state or government, minister, military officer, diplomat, legislator, intelligence or security official, or international organization.

\subsection{The Annual Update Cycle}

Adding a year requires (\emph{i}) recording the new XML URL, (\emph{ii}) running the download and parse scripts, (\emph{iii}) reviewing only the names that are new to the lookup files, and (\emph{iv}) re-running enrichment and analysis. Step (\emph{iii}) is the only manual one, and its cost falls over time. Heads of state, ministers, and senior American officials recur year after year, so each annual report adds proportionally fewer unmatched names. Table~\ref{tab:overview} shows the flip side: the newest period, 2019--2023, has the lowest linkage rate because its names have had the least review. In a living dataset, linkage rates are a release-specific quantity that should rise over time. In a static file, they are a permanent property of the data.

\input{tables/tab_overview}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_gifts_by_year.pdf}
\caption{Gifts reported per year (report year), 1999--2023. Vertical rules mark presidential transitions.}\label{fig:year}
\end{figure}

The current release contains \ngifts{} gifts reported between 1999 and 2023 (Table~\ref{tab:overview}). It covers 1,026 distinct recipients and 2,361 distinct givers with Wikidata identifiers, and givers from 169 countries. Seventy-one percent of gifts have a resolved recipient and 76\% a resolved giver. Ninety-four percent have a parseable dollar value; the median non-travel gift is worth about \$580, and the largest single item is a \$1,000,000 C.\,M.\ Russell painting presented by Saudi Arabia's ambassador to the First Family in 2002. About 11\% are gifts of travel or lodging, concentrated in Congress and the smaller executive agencies.

Figure~\ref{fig:year} shows the volume of reported gifts over time. Reports rose through the Obama administration, peaking at 722 in 2015, and then fell sharply: 4,291 gifts were reported for 2009--2016 against 1,549 for 2017--2023, with a low of 106 in 2020. The pandemic explains part of the 2020 trough. The 2017--2019 decline, however, began before the pandemic, and whether it reflects fewer gifts, less reporting, or changes in compilation is an open question that the data invite rather than answer. A 2024 Inspector General report found weak controls over foreign gifts \citep{gsaoig2024}. The figure also contains a measurement lesson: the 2015 spike is partly a backlog. The 2015 Senate report includes 243 gifts received years earlier, by members such as Joe Biden and Hillary Clinton while they were still senators. We therefore keep both the \emph{report year} and the \emph{receipt year} (available from the gift's date for 92\% of records). In about 5\% of records the two differ by more than a year.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_branch_multiples.pdf}
\caption{Gifts per year by branch of the reporting agency (report year). Panels share a y-axis. The Judicial branch (42 gifts) is omitted.}\label{fig:branch}
\end{figure}

The branch of the reporting agency structures almost everything about a gift (Table~\ref{tab:branch}, Figure~\ref{fig:branch}). The White House accounts for 37\% of gifts. These are the gifts of summit diplomacy, given overwhelmingly by heads of state and royalty and almost all resolvable to named people. Defense (18\%) and Diplomatic (16\%) agencies follow. Defense gifts flow largely from foreign military officers to American commanders, and their volume tracks the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, peaking around 2011. Congress (11\%) is distinctive in that 41\% of its reported gifts are travel, which reflects congressional delegations. The intelligence community (9\%) is almost entirely opaque: 99\% of its gifts list the giver only as ``5 U.S.C.\ 7342(f)(4),'' and only 35\% of its recipients are named. This is a substantive feature, not a parsing failure, and analysts should treat intelligence gifts as an \emph{institution-level} rather than a person-level record.

\subsection{Givers and Recipients by Level}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_role_branch.pdf}
\caption{Who gives to whom. Cells show the percentage of each recipient branch's gifts that come from each type of giver (rows sum to 100). Giver type is coded from honorifics and titles.}\label{fig:rolebranch}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:rolebranch} cross-tabulates the level of the giver against the branch of the recipient. The diagonal structure is striking: foreign governments match the rank and function of their counterpart. Heads of state and government account for 40\% of gifts to the White House, and royalty for another 18\%. Military officers account for 44\% of gifts to Defense. Ministers are spread across the White House, State, and Defense, consistent with their role as counterparts to cabinet secretaries. Foreign legislators are a small share of givers even to Congress. Most gifts to Congress come from heads of government, ministers, and unspecified officials, many of them hosting congressional delegations abroad. The pattern suggests that the gift record captures \emph{protocol-matched} contact: each tier of the U.S.\ government has a characteristic foreign counterpart. This is the kind of relationship that a network view of the data (Section~\ref{sec:apps}) makes visible.

\section{Who Receives Foreign Gifts?}\label{sec:recips}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\caption{Wikidata-linked recipients by branch of the reporting agency. A person who received gifts under several branches is counted in each. ``Female'' is the share of people with a recorded gender. ``Military'' means a recorded military rank (P410) or military occupation (P106). ``Diplomat'' and ``Law'' are occupation groups. ``Party member'' means any recorded party membership (P102). ``Studied abroad'' is the share of people with at least one school of known country who attended a school outside the United States. Missing statements count as absent, so shares other than ``Female'' and ``Studied abroad'' are lower bounds.}\label{tab:recipprofile}
\input{tables/tab_recip_profile}
\end{table}

The QIDs turn the gift record into a roster of the officials whom foreign governments cultivate. Table~\ref{tab:recipprofile} describes the 1,026 linked recipients using Wikidata statements (coverage is reported in Table~\ref{tab:wdcov}). The branches draw on distinct populations. Seventy-four percent of Defense recipients have a military career, and only 12\% are women. Seventy-one percent of Diplomatic recipients are recorded as diplomats, and 32\% are women, the highest share outside the White House. Legislative recipients are older (median birth year 1951), and 42\% are lawyers, as one would expect of members of Congress. The White House group is the youngest (median birth year 1961) and the most often female, because it includes first ladies, presidential children, and National Security Council staff.

Two columns speak directly to the study of bureaucracy. Party membership, recorded for 87\% of legislators, is recorded for only 30\% of Diplomatic and 17\% of Defense recipients. Absence of a party statement is not proof of a career appointment, but the gradient is consistent with the distinction between political appointees and career officials \citep{lewis2008politics}. The share who studied outside the United States is also low and varies by branch: 17\% at State and 7\% in Defense. As a result, a foreign official who wants a counterpart with shared educational experience will usually find one only by having studied in the United States. We return to this point below.

These profiles describe the \emph{linked} recipients, who are more prominent than the officials whose names could not be resolved. Assistant secretaries, deputy chiefs of mission, and colonels are less likely to have Wikidata items than secretaries and four-star officers, so the table is a portrait of the upper bureaucracy. Because the profile is rebuilt from the claims at each release, it will extend down the hierarchy as more officials are linked and as Wikidata adds items for them.

\section{What Do Givers and Recipients Share?}\label{sec:shared}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\caption{Characteristics shared by the giver and the recipient of each gift, compared with random pairings. The unit is a gift whose giver and recipient both have QIDs. ``Gifts'' counts those for which the characteristic is recorded for both people. The two baselines shuffle givers among gifts reported in the same year, or in the same branch and year, and average 500 permutations. ``Ratio'' is observed over the branch-year baseline. $p$ is the share of branch-year permutations at least as large as the observed value. ``Professional career'' groups occupations into military, diplomat, law, economics/business, academic, and civil servant (``politician'' is excluded). Panel B drops gifts reported by the White House and Congress.}\label{tab:shared}
\input{tables/tab_shared}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_shared.pdf}
\caption{Giver--recipient similarity relative to random pairing (the ratios in Table~\ref{tab:shared}). Diamonds compare the observed rate with random pairing within the same year; circles compare it with random pairing within the same branch and year. The distance between them is the part of the similarity explained by the office. Gray bars show the middle 95\% of the 500 branch-year permutations, so a circle outside its bar is unlikely to arise by chance. For a shared employer in the executive agencies, the bar extends below the axis because many permutations produce no matches.}\label{fig:shared}
\end{figure}

Because both parties to a gift carry QIDs, every gift is also a \emph{dyad} of two people whose characteristics can be compared. We compare each giver with the recipient on seven characteristics: gender, professional career, military service, birth cohort, the country and the specific institution where each was educated, and employer. Similarity alone is not evidence of anything, since the people who meet American officials are not a random draw from the world's elites. We therefore compare the observed rate of similarity with two random-pairing baselines (Table~\ref{tab:shared} and Figure~\ref{fig:shared}). The first shuffles givers among all gifts reported in the same year, which preserves the overall mix of givers and recipients. The second shuffles givers only within the same branch \emph{and} year, which also preserves the kind of foreign official each branch receives. The gap between the observed rate and the first baseline measures the total excess similarity. The gap between the observed rate and the second measures how much of it remains once the office is held fixed. That remainder is the part attributable to the sorting of \emph{people}.

\paragraph{Most similarity is institutional.} Givers and recipients share a professional career in 51.6\% of gifts, against 36.8\% under random pairing within the year. But pairing at random within branch and year already yields 48.7\%, so about four-fifths of the excess comes from the office. The same holds for military service: 13.6\% of gifts pass between two people with military careers, against 9.2\% at random and 13.0\% within branch. In Figure~\ref{fig:shared}, this appears as the wide gap between the diamonds and the circles for career and military service. This is the protocol matching of Section~\ref{sec:desc} (Figure~\ref{fig:rolebranch}) seen at the level of individuals. A foreign general gives to an American admiral because the admiral holds the office that receives foreign generals, not because of any personal affinity between the two.

\paragraph{Person-level similarity is real but modest.} Even against the branch-year baseline, observed similarity in gender, career, military service, and birth cohort is higher, by ratios of 1.02 to 1.08, and in all but one case fewer than 1\% of permutations match it. In the executive agencies (Panel~B), the excess is clearest for professional careers (62.3\% against 57.4\%) and for birth cohort (35.1\% against 32.9\%). Within the same office and year, foreign officials are slightly more likely to give to an American of the same profession and generation. Gender is a partial exception. Across all branches, same-gender pairs exceed the branch-year baseline by about five points, but in the executive agencies the excess is only one point. Gender matching is concentrated in the White House: 162 of the 233 woman-to-woman gifts went to White House recipients, most of them to first ladies and many from the spouses of foreign leaders.

\paragraph{Shared schooling is rare but striking.} Givers and recipients attended the same institution in fewer than 1\% of gifts. That share is still 1.65 times the branch-year baseline in the executive agencies ($p=0.01$). The cases are concentrated in elite American schools and in military education. Admiral Gary Roughead, Chief of Naval Operations, received four gifts in 2009--2011 from a Saudi naval officer, Prince Fahd bin Abdullah bin Mohammed Al Saud, who, like Roughead, attended the U.S.\ Naval Academy. Colin Powell (2001) and Joseph Ralston (1999) received gifts from foreign officers who had attended the Army Command and General Staff College: Bahrain's Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa and Georgia's David Tevzadze. Ambassador David Hale and King Abdullah II of Jordan are both graduates of Georgetown's School of Foreign Service. The giver side shows the size of this pool. Of the 1,526 linked givers whose schools are recorded, 288 (19\%) studied at an American institution, and they account for 22\% of gifts from givers with recorded schools. Twenty-seven attended an American service academy or staff or war college, among them Bahrain's Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, Egypt's Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Rwanda's Paul Kagame, and Indonesia's Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono. Such alumni are the people that research on educational exchange and professional military education expects to carry American ties into foreign governments \citep{atkinson2010soft,ruby2010pme,gift2017who}. The gift record shows some of them maintaining those ties with specific American counterparts.

\paragraph{Caveats.} The unit is the gift, so a pair that exchanges many gifts weighs more than a pair that exchanges one. Gifts are not independent, so the permutation $p$-values are descriptive. All seven comparisons depend on what Wikidata records. Coverage of education and employment is thinner for givers from some regions, and missing statements bias every match rate downward. This is also where the living design matters: the rates in Table~\ref{tab:shared} are recomputed from the claims at each release, so they will sharpen as Wikidata's coverage of foreign officials grows. The design extends naturally to richer measures of similarity, such as overlapping assignments, common postings, or shared membership in international bodies, all of which can be read from dated Wikidata positions.

\section{Technical, Business, and Political Backgrounds}\label{sec:backgrounds}

The officials on both sides of a gift arrive in office by different routes. Some are career politicians. Others are technocrats, such as economists, central bankers, civil servants, and officials of international organizations, and others come from the private sector. The background of an officeholder shapes policy \citep{adolph2013bankers,alexiadou2016ideologues,hallerberg2020economists}, and it may also shape whom an official deals with and how. This section classifies givers and recipients by background and by the office they held when the gift was exchanged, then asks whether technocrats, business people, and politicians exchange gifts with different counterparts and exchange different gifts.

\paragraph{Coding background and office.} We classify each person by the kind of work that fills most of their recorded career. From the dated positions (P39) and employers (P108) in Wikidata, we count the calendar years each person spent in four kinds of work:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Political:} elected office, heads of state and government, cabinet posts, and royalty.
\item \emph{Technical:} central banks, finance ministries, international organizations, sub-cabinet and diplomatic posts, the judiciary, and employment by a government agency, university, or research institute.
\item \emph{Business:} employment by a firm, or posts such as chief executive.
\item \emph{Military:} commands and ranks.
\end{itemize}
Overlapping jobs are counted once, an undated job counts as four years, and a general or flag rank counts as a full military career. The primary background is the kind of work with the most years. Under this rule, a lawyer who spent most of a career in elected office is political (Barack Obama, Joe Biden, Mike Pompeo). A politician whose career was mainly in business is business (Donald Trump, Silvio Berlusconi, Rex Tillerson, Steven Mnuchin), and a central banker or international civil servant who entered politics is technical (Mario Draghi, Ban Ki-moon). Spouses and children of leaders form a separate category, because they receive and give gifts through family rather than career. People with no classifiable job fall back on occupation and education codes. Table~\ref{tab:bgprofile} also reports three overlapping indicators, which flag any technical occupation, education, or position, any business occupation, and any political career.

The office is coded at the time of the gift. For recipients it follows the reporting agency: the White House and Congress are political offices, State and USAID diplomatic, Defense, the intelligence community, and Homeland Security security offices, and the remaining executive agencies and the courts technical. For givers it follows the title in the gift report. Finance ministers, central bankers, directors-general, commissioners, and officials of international organizations hold technical offices. Executives of firms hold business offices. Heads of state, ministers, and legislators hold political offices, and officers and diplomats hold security and diplomatic offices.

\centering\footnotesize
\caption{Backgrounds of Wikidata-linked recipients and givers. The indicators overlap; the primary background is the kind of work that fills most of a person's recorded career (see text). ``Unknown'' means Wikidata records no classifiable job or occupation.}\label{tab:bgprofile}
\input{tables/tab_bg_profile}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Who has which background.} The recipient and giver populations differ (Table~\ref{tab:bgprofile}). A third of linked American recipients are technocrats by career, about the same share as politicians, and a fifth are military officers. Foreign givers are much more often politicians (48\%), reflecting the heads of state, ministers, and legislators who dominate summit diplomacy, and only 11\% are technocrats. Business careers are rare on both sides: 4\% of recipients and 2\% of givers.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\caption{Who gives to whom, by primary background. Gifts whose giver and recipient both have a known background. Each cell shows the percentage of the row's gifts going to each recipient background, with the ratio to the share expected if givers and recipients were matched independently in parentheses. Ratios above 1 mean more gifts than expected.}\label{tab:bgmatrix}
\input{tables/tab_bg_matrix}

\bigskip
\caption{Who gives to whom, by office at the time of the gift. All gifts with a classifiable giver office. Cells as in Table~\ref{tab:bgmatrix}.}\label{tab:officematrix}
\input{tables/tab_office_matrix}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Who exchanges gifts with whom.} Gifts pass between like backgrounds more often than independent matching would predict (Table~\ref{tab:bgmatrix}). The pattern is strongest for spouses and family, who give to their American counterparts at 5.4 times the expected rate, and for military officers (2.7). It is weaker but present for business (1.7) and technical (1.2) careers. Givers with business careers are also overrepresented among gifts to American technocrats (1.4) and underrepresented among gifts to military officers (0.4). Political givers spread their gifts across recipient types almost in proportion. Sorting by office is far sharper than sorting by background (Table~\ref{tab:officematrix}). Foreign officials in technical offices direct 38\% of their gifts to American technical agencies, 5.8 times the expected share, whereas political officeholders direct only 3\% of theirs there. Security offices give 87\% of their gifts to American security agencies. The few givers in business offices give mostly to technical agencies and to the State Department. As in Section~\ref{sec:shared}, the office does most of the sorting. Background adds a weaker, person-level layer on top of it.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\scriptsize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\caption{The nature and value of gifts by the background of the giver and of the recipient. Median value and the share over \$5,000 exclude travel. Gift types are coded from the item description by keyword; the remaining 12\% of gifts (pens, desk sets, and miscellany) are not shown.}\label{tab:bggifts}
\input{tables/tab_bg_gifts}
\end{table}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize
\caption{Log estimated value of a gift regressed on giver and recipient backgrounds and giver office, with branch and year fixed effects. Gifts with both parties linked and a known background, excluding travel. The reference category is political for each set of indicators. Standard errors are clustered by giver. ``Value ratio'' is $\exp(\beta)$, the multiplicative difference in value relative to the reference.}\label{tab:bgvalue}
\input{tables/tab_bg_value}
\end{table}

\paragraph{The nature and value of gifts.} What is given differs more by background than how much (Tables~\ref{tab:bggifts} and~\ref{tab:bgvalue}). Givers with business careers give the most valuable gifts at the median (\$728) and most often give gifts worth more than \$5,000 (10\%), and they give textiles and clothing far more often than other givers (19\%). Military givers favor weapons and ceremonial items such as swords, daggers, and medals (16\%). Spouses and family give jewelry (26\%) and receive it (31\%). Watches go disproportionately to American military officers (14\% of their gifts). Once the branch and year are held fixed, however, most differences in value are small and imprecise. Gifts from business givers are about 20\% more valuable than gifts from political givers, but the estimate is not distinguishable from zero. Gifts from military givers are about a third less valuable, and gifts from foreign diplomats about 30\% less valuable, than gifts from political officeholders. The recipient's background makes little difference to value once the branch is known. Foreign governments appear to scale the value of a gift to the office and the occasion, and to tailor its form to the person.

\paragraph{Caveats.} Business careers are rare, so the business estimates rest on a few hundred gifts. The classification depends on Wikidata's dated positions and employers. These are fuller for prominent people and for Western countries, and a fifth of givers have no classifiable career. The office codes for givers rely on titles in the gift reports, and a quarter of giver offices cannot be classified. Gift types are coded by keyword. All of these codes are stored in the analysis script, and the classification is recomputed at each release, so it will improve as Wikidata records more of each official's career.

\section{The Wikidata Identifier as a Linking Key}\label{sec:link}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Share of Wikidata-linked recipients and givers for whom Wikidata supplies each attribute (from a snapshot of statements for all linked QIDs).}\label{tab:wdcov}
\input{tables/tab_wikidata_coverage}
\end{table}

A QID is a join key and a gateway at once. As a gateway, it connects each gift to whatever Wikidata knows about the people involved. Table~\ref{tab:wdcov} shows that, for linked recipients, Wikidata supplies gender for 98\%, occupation for 91\%, education for 88\%, date of birth for 85\%, and at least one dated position for 59\%. Coverage of givers is similar. Collecting these covariates by hand for 3,400 people in some 170 countries would be a project in itself. Through the QID they arrive with one batched API call per 50 people.

\subsection{Joining to the Comparative Legislators Database}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Recipients and givers who ever held a seat in a chamber covered by the Comparative Legislators Database, identified from Wikidata positions held (P39). These people can be joined to the CLD on \texttt{wikidataid} with no name matching.}\label{tab:cld}
\input{tables/tab_cld_link}
\end{table}

The Comparative Legislators Database \citep{gobel2022cld} assembles individual-level data on more than 67,000 legislators in 16 countries and keys every legislator to both a Wikipedia page ID and a Wikidata ID. Because the CLD and our data share that key, linking them is an exact join. Table~\ref{tab:cld} shows the scale of the overlap. Two hundred forty-seven of our recipients served in the U.S.\ House or Senate at some point, and they account for 2,314 gifts, including gifts received \emph{after} leaving Congress, as Secretaries of State, Vice Presidents, or CIA directors. On the giver side, 179 foreign officials sat in a CLD chamber, led by members of the Italian Chamber of Deputies (22 people, 164 gifts), the Japanese House of Representatives (31 people, 92 gifts), and the French National Assembly. Once joined, a researcher has, for each legislator-recipient, the CLD's political histories, committee and office records, and Wikipedia traffic, alongside the gifts that person received. With the CLD's R interface \citep{legislatoR}, the join takes a few lines:

\begin{lstlisting}[language=R,caption={Joining gift recipients to the CLD (R).}]
library(legislatoR); library(dplyr)
gifts  <- read.csv("analysis/output/gifts_analysis.csv")
house  <- get_core(legislature = "usa_house")      # one row per legislator
senate <- get_core(legislature = "usa_senate")
congress <- bind_rows(house, senate) |> distinct(wikidataid, .keep_all = TRUE)

linked <- gifts |>
  inner_join(congress, by = c("recip_wiki" = "wikidataid"))   # exact key, no fuzzy match
\end{lstlisting}

The same logic extends beyond the CLD. Any dataset that carries QIDs, or that can be crosswalked to them once, becomes joinable. For leaders, the giving side of the gift relationship could be matched to leader-level resources such as Archigos \citep{goemans2009archigos} and LEAD \citep{ellis2015lead}: the match is done once, at the level of a few hundred heads of state, and the QID then carries it to every gift. Donor and ideology data such as DIME \citep{bonica2014mapping} could be crosswalked the same way for American recipients. For countries, the ISO codes stored on Wikidata country items connect the country-year panel to standard cross-national data through existing converters \citep{arelbundock2018countrycode}.

\subsection{Why the Key Matters for Living Data}

Persistent identifiers also make the link durable. If our data and the CLD both update, the join still works, because neither project's internal row numbers or name spellings matter. By contrast, a crosswalk built between two static files on names breaks as soon as either file is revised. The QID moves the work of maintaining identity out of individual research projects and into a shared, openly edited resource. When a Wikidata editor merges two duplicate items for the same person, every project keyed to that person benefits.

\section{Office Versus Officeholder}\label{sec:office}
